etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English myschef, meschef, meschief, mischef, from Old French meschief, from meschever (“to bring to grief”), from mes- (“badly”) + chever (“happen; come to a head”), from Vulgar Latin *capare, from Latin caput (“head”).

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Conduct that playfully causes petty annoyance.
(collective) A group or a pack of rats.

quote.citation: 2014, G. W. Rennie, The Rat Chronicles, iUniverse, →ISBN, page 21:
quote.text: Kirac, the leader of the rats under his charge, speaks to the major through his telepathic abilities that manifested after the alien virus infected him and his mischief of rats.

quote.citation: 2015, Rachel Smith, John Davidson, Rats For Kids, Mendon Cottage Books, →ISBN, page 6:
quote.text: A group of rats is not a herd or a gaggle, but a pack or a mischief of rats. Rats in general are omnivorous, meaning they will eat almost anything.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Harm or trouble caused by an agent or brought about by a particular cause.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “The Tenth Book of the Æneis”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, page 502, lines 139–140:
quote.text: Was I the Cauſe of Miſchief, or the Man / Whoſe lawlesſ Luſt the bloody War began?

quote.citation: 1718 December 15 (Gregorian calendar), Jonathan Swift, “A Letter Concerning the Sacramental Test”, in Thomas Sheridan, John Nichols, editors, The Works of the Rev. Jonathan Swift, […], new edition, volume IV, London:  […]  J[oseph] Johnson, […], published 1801, →OCLC, page 435:
quote.text: I have been tired in history with the perpetual folly of those states, who call in foreigners to assist them against a common enemy: but the mischief was, these allies would never be brought to allow, that the common enemy was quite subdued. And they had reason; for it proved at last, that one part of the common enemy was those who called them in, and so the allies became at length the masters.

quote.citation: 1815 December (indicated as 1816), [Jane Austen], chapter 8, in Emma: […], volume I, London:  […]  [Charles Roworth and James Moyes] for John Murray, →OCLC:
quote.text: Vanity working on a weak head, produces every sort of mischief.

quote.citation: 1914 September – 1915 May, Arthur Conan Doyle, chapter 1, in The Valley of Fear: A Sherlock Holmes Novel, New York, N.Y.: George H[enry] Doran Company, published 27 February 1915, →OCLC:
quote.text: I fear this means that there is some mischief afoot.

definitions.definition: (countable) An injury or an instance of harm or trouble caused by a person or other agent or cause.

quote.citation: c. 1589–1590 (date written), Christopher Marlo[we], edited by Tho[mas] Heywood, The Famous Tragedy of the Rich Iew of Malta. […], London:  […]  I[ohn] B[eale] for Nicholas Vavasour, […], published 1633, →OCLC, Act I:
1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Deuteronomy 32:23:
quote.text: I will heape mischiefes vpon them, I will spend mine arrowes vpon them.

definitions.definition: (law) A criminal offence defined in various ways in various jurisdictions, sometimes including causing damage to another's property.
(archaic, countable) A cause or agent of annoyance, harm or injury, especially a person who causes mischief.

quote.citation: 1753 (indicated as 1754), [Samuel Richardson], The History of Sir Charles Grandison. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London:  […]  S[amuel] Richardson; [a]nd sold by C. Hitch and L. Hawes, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: To die like a man of honour, Sir Hargrave, you must have lived like one. You should be sure of your cause. But these pistols are too ready a mischief. Were I to meet you in your own way, Sir Hargrave, I should not expect, that a man so enraged would fire his over my head, as I should be willing to do mine over his. Life I would not put upon the perhaps involuntary twitch of a finger.

quote.citation: 1993, Carlos Parada, Genealogic Guide to Greek Mythology‎[1], page 71:
quote.text: Epimetheus was scatter-brained and a mischief to men for having taken the woman [Pandora] that Zeus had formed.

definitions.definition: (euphemistic) The Devil; used as an expletive.

quote.text: What the mischief are you? and how the mischief did you get here, and where in thunder did you come from?

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To do a mischief to; to harm.

quote.citation: 1719, Daniel Defoe, The Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, page 144:
quote.text: […]  so, when the two ladders were taken down, no man living could come down to me without mischiefing himself,  […]

quote.citation: 1911, James Matthew Barrie, Peter and Wendy, page 86:
quote.text: 'Not now, Smee,' Hook said darkly. 'He is only one, and I want to mischief all the seven. Scatter and look for them.'
And so it hath been divers times; Men mischiefing the Jews to excuse their own Wickedness: as to instance one Precedent in the time of a certain King of Portugal.
